objectives: State the principles of stereo + surround imaging.
Distinguish binaural from object-based spatial audio.

slides.title: Stereo + spatial perception
slides.body:
Humans localize sound via:
- **Interaural Time Difference (ITD)**: sound arrives at one ear before the other. Most useful at LOW frequencies (<1500 Hz; longer wavelengths, sound diffracts around head).
- **Interaural Level Difference (ILD)**: head shadows the further ear. Useful at HIGH frequencies (>1500 Hz).
- **HRTF (Head-Related Transfer Function)**: ear pinna + head shape filter sound differently from each direction. Provides ELEVATION + FRONT/BACK cues.
- **Movement + head turning**: small head movements + the resulting ITD/ILD changes resolve front/back ambiguity.

**Stereo** (2-channel L/R): can place sounds in a horizontal arc between speakers using:
- **Panning** (level difference between L/R): main tool. Pan law = 'how much loss when centered'. Common: -3 dB equal-power, -6 dB constant-amplitude.
- **Time offset** (Haas effect, <30 ms): listener perceives the sound at the EARLIER speaker. Used sparingly for stereo widening.
- **Spectral cues** (high-end widening): subtle EQ differences L/R give a 'wider' sense.

**Stereo width**:
- Mono content: dead center between speakers.
- Hard-panned: speaker location.
- Wide stereo: M/S processing exaggerates side content.

**Phase + correlation**:
- L+R in phase: mono-compatible. Folds to mono cleanly.
- L-R counter-phase: anti-phase. Folds to ZERO (silence) in mono — a problem on TV / phone speakers, AM radio.
- Phase meters in mixers show correlation. Aim for positive correlation.

**Pan law**: when something is panned center, it plays at full level in BOTH L + R. At hard-pan (100% L), only L speaker. Equal-power: -3 dB at center reduces total power so center + hard-panned content have same loudness.

**Stereo speakers (equilateral triangle)**: ideal listener position is the 'sweet spot' — apex of equilateral triangle with speakers. Outside this, imaging shifts. Headphones eliminate this — each ear gets dedicated channel.

slides.title: Surround + 5.1 / 7.1 + Atmos
slides.body:
**Surround sound formats**:

**5.1**: front L/R, center, back L/R, LFE (.1, subwoofer). Standard for movie theaters since 1990s + home theater.
- Center channel: dialogue anchored to screen.
- Surround speakers: ambient environment, effects, music.
- LFE: very low frequencies (<120 Hz) routed to dedicated sub.

**7.1**: 5.1 + side L/R surrounds. More precise lateral imaging.

**7.1.4 (Dolby Atmos for home)**: 7.1 + 4 height speakers (or speaker-mounted height drivers). Allows sound elevation.

**9.1.6, 11.1.8** etc: enterprise + cinematic configurations.

**Atmos (Dolby Atmos)**: OBJECT-BASED rather than channel-based. Mix audio as 3D positioned objects; renderer maps to whatever speaker layout user has (2.0, 5.1, 7.1.4, headphones via binaural). Future-proof.

Objects: each sound element has 3D position + size + level metadata. Renderer (decoder in playback chain) places it on whichever speakers fit.

**Atmos workflow**:
1. Compose / mix in spatial audio DAW (Dolby Atmos Music tools, Pro Tools Atmos).
2. Send tracks as either objects (positioned in 3D) or beds (traditional channels — 7.1.2 + 7.1.4).
3. Render to deliverables: ADM BWF (Atmos Distribution Master), MP4 with Atmos metadata for streaming.

**Atmos Music**: Apple Music, Tidal, Amazon Music HD all support Atmos. Many top releases since 2021 have Atmos mixes. Quality + technique still evolving.

**Ambisonics**: spherical-harmonic encoding of 3D soundfield. Microphones (Soundfield, Sennheiser AMBEO) capture; decoder converts to whatever output (binaural, speakers). Used in VR + 360 video. Encoding is order-N: 0th (mono), 1st (4-channel), 3rd (16-channel), higher = more precise localization.

**Binaural rendering**: HRTF-convolution converts spatial audio to 2-channel headphone output that gives 3D illusion. Works well for headphones. Apple Spatial Audio uses this; many Atmos releases auto-binaural.

slides.title: Binaural + HRTF + the headphone problem
slides.body:
**Headphones**: each ear gets ONE channel. To create spatial illusion: apply HRTF (head-related transfer function) to position-shift the sound.

**HRTF**: how an individual's ears + head + torso filter sound from each direction. Unique per person (ear shape varies). Captured via dummy-head measurements (KEMAR, Neumann KU-100) or in-ear microphones.

**Generic vs personalized HRTFs**:
- Generic (from KEMAR dummy): works for everyone OK; not exact.
- Personalized (3D-scan your ear + ML predict your HRTF): more accurate. Apple's AirPods Pro + iPhone do this with a face/ear scan.

**Binaural recordings**: stereo recordings made WITH HRTF baked in — typically a dummy head with two in-ear microphones. Played back on headphones, sound 3D realistic. Famous demos (Virtual Barber Shop) showcase.

**Spatial cues**:
- **ITD**: head circumference / speed of sound × angle. ~0.6 ms max ITD between ears.
- **ILD**: high-frequency shadow can be 20+ dB at 90° azimuth.
- **Pinna filtering**: notches + peaks differ for elevation + front/back. Critical cues for these directions.
- **Reverberation**: distance cues via direct-to-reverb ratio + reverb time.
- **Doppler**: moving sources shift pitch (rare in music; common in cinema).

**VR / AR spatial audio**:
- Head tracking: sound source should stay PLACED in space as user turns head. Tech: head-tracked spatial audio (Apple AirPods Pro 2 + iPhone gyroscopes).
- Sound objects + ambient + music layered for immersion.
- Spatial audio crucial to VR presence (mismatch with visual = breaks immersion + can cause motion sickness).

**Spatial audio tools**:
- Dolby Atmos Renderer (DAR): authoring + monitoring.
- Steinberg / Nuendo: Atmos tools.
- Pro Tools Ultimate: Atmos integrated.
- Apple Logic Pro: Atmos workflow.
- Plugins: FB360 Spatial Workstation, Waves NX, Wave Arts Convology XT.

**Future**: AI-generated HRTFs from photo of ear, AR-based personal spatial audio + the metaverse drive growing investment.

question.question: Compute ITD for a sound source
question.goal: Sound source at 60° to the listener's right. Head width ~17 cm. Speed of sound ~343 m/s.

steps.prompt: ITD ≈ (head radius × angle) / speed-of-sound. Path-length difference: head radius × sin(angle) (Woodworth's formula). Compute the difference for 60° + 0.085 m radius.

steps.reveal: ~215 μs (0.215 ms). The right ear hears the sound this much later than the left.
~248 μs at 90°. Just over 0.6 ms (if including ear-to-back path differences). The maximum ITD humans use for localization. Below ~1500 Hz where wavelength > head size, ITD is the dominant cue.

question.finalResult: $$\boxed{\text{ITD} \approx (r/c) \sin(\theta), \text{ max ~0.6 ms}}$$ The brain decodes ITD with remarkable precision — humans can detect ITD differences as small as ~10 μs! Combined with ILD (level difference, dominant at high frequencies), pinna filtering (elevation + front/back), reverberation (distance), the brain builds a rich 3D auditory scene. Binaural recordings + HRTF processing exploit all of this to create headphone-based spatial illusion.

question.question: Why is Atmos called 'object-based' rather than 'channel-based'?
options: Sounds are stored as positioned objects with 3D metadata (x, y, z, size); the renderer at playback positions them on WHATEVER speaker configuration the listener has (2.0 stereo, 5.1, 7.1.4, headphones via binaural). Future-proof: same master plays on any layout.
question.explanation: Channel-based: master mixed for specific speaker layout (5.1). Plays correctly only on that layout. Object-based (Atmos): master = objects + metadata. Renderer adapts to any layout. Same master plays on 2.0 (stereo collapse), 5.1, 7.1.4, headphones (binaural). Future-proof for new layouts. Increased flexibility + production complexity. Apple Music + Tidal + Amazon all stream Atmos Music. Growing share of new releases (2021+) include Atmos.

slides.workedSolution: Channel-based: mix tailored to specific speaker layout. 5.1 mix needs 5.1 system; on stereo, manual downmix degrades quality. Object-based: objects + positional metadata → renderer adapts to listener's gear (stereo, 5.1, 7.1.4, binaural). Same mix scales. Increased authoring complexity but future-proof; Atmos rapidly becoming the spatial standard.

question.prompt: Designing audio for a 360° VR game with head-tracked spatial audio. Walk through choices: ambisonics vs object-based vs binaural rendering.
Explain in two or three sentences why object-based spatial audio (Atmos) is replacing channel-based formats (5.1) as the production standard.
question.rubric: Mentions that object-based mixes play on ANY speaker configuration via render-side adaptation; channel-based mixes lock in a specific layout + degrade when downmixed; Atmos future-proofs for new layouts + headphones; integrated workflow (DAWs support natively) makes it tractable. Industry transition is well-underway in cinematic + music (Apple Music, Tidal streaming Atmos by default).
